sections.title: Advanced Filtering — IN, NOT IN, LIKE, BETWEEN

blocks.md: **The sentence you will rewrite most often in interviews:** "Show me customers who signed up in January but never placed an order." Filtering is the first draft of half the SQL you will ever write.
**WHERE is your precision tool. IN for lists, LIKE for patterns, BETWEEN for ranges. Chain with AND/OR — parentheses control precedence.**

steps: **dept_id IN (1, 3, 5)** → keeps rows whose department is in the list
**first_name LIKE 'A%'** → keeps rows whose name starts with A
**AND** → both must survive; one predicate can veto a row
**ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5** → the survivors, ranked, capped

blocks.label: IN / NOT IN
blocks.py-pandas:
# IN
e = employees[employees['dept_id'].isin([1, 3, 5])]

# NOT IN
e = employees[~employees['dept_id'].isin([2, 4])]

# Subquery
yc_depts = departments[departments['location'] == 'NYC']['id']
e = employees[employees['dept_id'].isin(yc_depts)]

blocks.claim: WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM contractors) returns everyone who is not a contractor — the opposite of IN, exactly like NOT EXISTS.
blocks.refutation: This is false — and it is the most expensive typo in SQL. If the subquery's column holds even one NULL, every row's NOT IN test evaluates to UNKNOWN, WHERE discards every row, and the query silently returns **zero rows** instead of "everyone else". NOT EXISTS has no such trap: it tests row-by-row existence and treats NULLs safely.
blocks.correctModel: NOT IN over a nullable subquery is a NULL bomb. Either guarantee the column is NOT NULL, filter the NULLs out of the subquery, or reach for NOT EXISTS / an anti-join.
blocks.cue: Ask: can the subquery column be NULL? One NULL in the list poisons the whole IN.

evidence.label: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS on hr — manager_id holds the CEO's NULL
evidence.code:
-- The subquery picks up the CEO's NULL manager_id...
SELECT count(*) AS not_in_count
FROM   employees
WHERE  emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees);
-- ...so NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and returns 0.

-- NOT EXISTS answers the same intent safely: emp_ids nobody manages
SELECT count(*) AS not_exists_count
FROM   employees e
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees m
                   WHERE  m.manager_id = e.emp_id);

blocks.label: LIKE patterns
blocks.pg:
-- Case-insensitive
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name ILIKE 'a%';
blocks.mysql:
-- Case-insensitive (default in MySQL)
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name LIKE 'a%';
blocks.py-pandas:
# Starts with
e = employees[employees['name'].str.startswith('A')]

# Ends with
e = employees[employees['email'].str.endswith('@company.com')]

# Contains
e = employees[employees['name'].str.contains('son')]

# Regex for single char
e = employees[employees['name'].str.match(r'^J.n$')]
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Starts with
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.like('A%')).all()

# Ends with
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.email.like('%@company.com')).all()

# Contains
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.like('%son%')).all()

# Case-insensitive
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.name.ilike('a%')).all()

sections.title: Compound Conditions — AND, OR, NOT, Precedence

blocks.label: boolean logic
blocks.code:
-- AND has higher precedence than OR
-- This: salary > 50000 AND dept = 1 OR dept = 2
-- Means: (salary > 50000 AND dept = 1) OR dept = 2

-- Use parentheses for clarity
SELECT * FROM employees 
WHERE (salary > 50000 AND dept_id = 1) 
   OR (salary > 60000 AND dept_id = 2);

-- NOT
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE NOT (dept_id = 3 OR salary < 30000);
blocks.py-pandas:
# Parentheses for precedence
e = employees[
    ((employees['salary'] > 50000) & (employees['dept_id'] == 1)) |
    ((employees['salary'] > 60000) & (employees['dept_id'] == 2))
]

# NOT
e = employees[~((employees['dept_id'] == 3) | (employees['salary'] < 30000))]
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Parentheses
from sqlalchemy import or_, and_
session.query(Employee).filter(
    or_(
        and_(Employee.salary > 50000, Employee.dept_id == 1),
        and_(Employee.salary > 60000, Employee.dept_id == 2)
    )
).all()

# NOT
session.query(Employee).filter(
    ~or_(Employee.dept_id == 3, Employee.salary < 30000)
).all()

items.q: Because AND binds tighter than OR, the expression A AND B OR C parses as…
items.explain: AND binds tighter than OR. Use parentheses to be explicit.

items.q: Applying De Morgan's law, NOT (A OR B) becomes…
items.explain: De Morgan's law: NOT (A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.

blocks.md: EXPLAIN shows how the database *will* execute your query. It reveals: scan type (Seq Scan vs Index Scan), join method, estimated cost, and row counts. At L2, focus on: **Seq Scan = full table read (slow for large tables), Index Scan = targeted lookup (fast)**.
**Cost dropped from 185 → 42. Time from 12ms → 3ms.** Index Scan reads only matching rows; Seq Scan reads entire table. At L3 you'll learn when indexes *don't* help.

items.explain: Sequential Scan = full table scan. Reads all pages sequentially.

options: A full scan of the index itself
items.explain: Index Cond shows the condition applied during index lookup.

blocks.sql: SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM employees;
blocks.pg: SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name FROM employees;
blocks.mysql: SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name FROM employees;

blocks.md: **ANSI & PostgreSQL use ||. MySQL uses CONCAT().** In MySQL, || is logical OR unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT mode enabled.

blocks.title: B201 dry run — FROM → WHERE (IN) → ORDER BY → LIMIT

stages.label: FROM
stages.sql: SELECT emp_id, first_name, dept_id, salary FROM employees ORDER BY emp_id;
stages.note: Logical step 1 — **FROM** produces the full grid: all 21 employees in hr (12 in the edge twin), no filtering yet.

stages.label: WHERE
stages.sql: SELECT emp_id, first_name, dept_id, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (1, 3, 5) ORDER BY emp_id;
stages.note: **WHERE** keeps only rows whose department is in the list — 10 of 21 employees survive in hr (6 of 12 in the edge twin).

stages.label: ORDER BY
stages.sql: SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (1, 3, 5) ORDER BY salary DESC;
stages.note: **ORDER BY** ranks the survivors highest salary first — the row set has not changed, only its order.

stages.label: LIMIT
stages.sql: SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (1, 3, 5) ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 5;
stages.note: **LIMIT** caps the result at 5 rows — the final answer. Each stage is a complete query showing the intermediate table.

items.title: Employees in Dept 1, 3, or 5
items.statement: List all employees in departments 1 (Executive), 3 (Sales) or 5 (Finance). Expected: all employee columns, exactly the 10 rows in hr (6 in the edge twin), any order. The trace above is the dry run of the optimal approach.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Spell the list as an OR chain — one equality per department.
approaches.cost: same scan as the optimal form — the planner rewrites OR-of-equalities into a membership test
approaches.pitfalls: Adding a department means editing the WHERE line again; a 12-item list becomes unreadable.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: IN states the membership test in one token and reads like the requirement.
approaches.cost: identical plan — one seq scan with the same filter
approaches.pitfalls: IN over a *subquery* has the NULL poison trap (see the misconception above); over a literal list it is perfectly safe.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for employees in departments 1, 3 or 5.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (1, 3, 5);

followups.q: When is OR-of-equalities actually better than IN?
followups.a: When the list is built dynamically or each member needs a different operator — e.g. dept_id = 1 OR salary > 200000. For a flat membership test, IN is clearer.

followups.q: Does IN use an index when one exists on dept_id?
followups.a: Yes — the planner can turn IN (1, 3, 5) into a Bitmap Index Scan, one probe per list item.

items.title: Names Starting with 'A' or 'B'
items.statement: Find employees whose first name starts with A or B. Expected: all employee columns for the 3 matching rows in hr (1 in the edge twin), any order.
hints: Use LIKE 'A%' OR LIKE 'B%' or SIMILAR TO

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for employees whose first_name starts with A or B.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE first_name LIKE 'A%' OR first_name LIKE 'B%';

items.title: Top 3 by Salary in Each Dept (Conceptual)
items.statement: Write the query pattern to get the top 3 salaries *per department*. (Full solution arrives with window functions at L3 — here, reason about why ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC LIMIT 3 is wrong: it returns the global top 3 after one grouping, never the top 3 *within* each department.)
hints: ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC LIMIT 3 — but this gives global top 3, not per dept
You need a ranking that restarts per department — that is exactly what ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id …) does at L3

items.title: Pagination: Page 2 (10 per page)
items.statement: Get the second page of employees ordered by emp_id, 10 per page. Expected: all employee columns, rows 11–20 (10 rows in hr, 2 in the edge twin). Ordering by the unique key emp_id makes the page deterministic — hire_date would leave ties at the boundary.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for the second page of employees ordered by emp_id, 10 rows per page.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY emp_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;

items.title: Exclude Departments 4 and 6
items.statement: All employees NOT in departments 4 (Marketing) or 6 (HR). Expected: all employee columns, 16 rows in hr (10 in the edge twin), any order. Literal lists are safe from the NULL trap — only subqueries can carry a NULL into NOT IN.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for employees not in departments 4 or 6.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept_id NOT IN (4, 6);

items.title: Email Domain Filter
items.statement: Employees with a company email — every address in the data ends in @acme.io. Expected: all employee columns, 18 rows in hr (10 in the edge twin), any order. NULL emails (three in hr) never match LIKE — they simply drop out.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for employees whose email ends with @acme.io.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE email LIKE '%@acme.io';

glossary.def: Sequential scan — reads every table page; O(N) cost.
Uses B-tree index to jump directly to matching rows; O(log N) + matches.
% (any chars) and _ (one char) in LIKE patterns.
Order of operations: NOT > AND > OR. Parentheses override.
LIMIT n OFFSET m — skip m rows, take n. Page k = OFFSET k*page_size.
